title: Visual Texts: Advertisements and Cartoons
summary: How advertisements persuade (target audience, slogans, persuasive techniques, images and layout) and how cartoons create humour and make a point, using described examples.

notes.text: An **advertisement** aims to **persuade** people to buy a product, use a service or support an idea. Advertisers think carefully about their **target audience**: the group of people they want to reach (by age, gender, interests or income).

notes.caption: Parts of an advertisement
rows: Shows the product or creates an attractive feeling
Gives more information about the product
A short, catchy, memorable phrase linked to the brand
Tells the reader what to do: 'Buy now!', 'Visit our website'
'Give your family the love they deserve.'
A famous athlete using the product
'Buy one, get one free!' 'Limited time only'
A cereal advert: 'Start your day the grain way.'

notes.title: Described advertisement (original)
notes.text: The advert shows a smiling teenage girl in a school uniform drinking from a bright green bottle, with sunlight behind her. The headline in large yellow letters reads: STAY FRESH. STAY FOCUSED. Below it: 'ZING Energy Water: packed with vitamins to power you through every test.' In the bottom corner is a small logo of a lightning bolt and the slogan 'ZING. Think fast.' Tiny print at the very bottom says: 'Contains caffeine. Not recommended for children under 16.'

notes.label: Think critically
notes.text: Always ask: What is the advert **not** telling me? In the ZING advert, the warning about caffeine is in tiny print, although the advert shows a learner who may be under 16.

notes.title: Spotting the technique
notes.problem: An advert shows a famous soccer star drinking a soft drink, with the words 'Champions drink Zing'. Which technique is used?
steps: A celebrity is used to make the product attractive: endorsement.
'Champions' suggests that you will be a winner: emotional appeal to success.
notes.answer: Celebrity endorsement and an appeal to the desire for success.

notes.text: A **cartoon** uses drawings, often with speech bubbles, to entertain or to make a point about an issue. Cartoons create humour through **exaggeration**, **irony**, **puns** and unexpected situations.

items: **Speech bubbles**: words spoken by a character.
**Body language and facial expressions**: show feelings such as anger, surprise or embarrassment.
**Font**: bold or large letters show shouting or emphasis.
**Frames**: a comic strip tells a story in a sequence of frames.

notes.title: Described cartoon (original)
notes.text:
Frame 1: A father sits on the couch, staring at his cellphone. His son says, 'Dad, can we talk?' The father answers, without looking up, 'Not now, I'm busy.'
Frame 2: The son sits down and sends a message on his own phone.
Frame 3: The father's phone buzzes. He reads: 'Dad, can we talk?' He looks shocked, his eyes wide.

notes.title: Explaining the humour
notes.problem: Explain the humour and message of the cartoon.
steps: Humour: it is ironic that the son, sitting right next to his father, can only get his attention by sending a text message.
The father's wide eyes in frame 3 show his shock at realising this.
Message: people (even parents) spend so much time on their phones that they neglect face-to-face communication with their families.
notes.answer: The humour comes from irony; the message criticises phone addiction.

Who is the target audience of the ZING advertisement?
'Join the thousands of learners who already use our app!' Which technique is used?

Why do you think the caffeine warning in the ZING advert is in tiny print?

✓ because it might stop people, especially the young learners shown, from buying the drink (1)
